dimensions.question: When will AI do most cognitive work at the level of top human experts?
dimensions.note: Each person's own milestone is used when it is close to this; the placement says which.

points.label: By the end of 2027
After 2040, or not on any foreseeable timeline

dimensions.question: Once that capability exists, how quickly does it transform the economy and society?

points.label: Within about a year (an intelligence explosion)
Within a few years
Over roughly a decade
Over several decades, like past general-purpose technologies
Explosive: far above any historical rate (roughly 10%+ a year, sustained)
Much faster than today, but not explosive
Gains comparable to past technology waves
Little measurable change for a long time

dimensions.question: How likely is an AI catastrophe (extinction, permanent loss of human control, or comparable)?
dimensions.note: Placed only from a stated probability or an explicit verbal equivalent.

points.label: More likely than not (over 50%)
Substantial (roughly 10% to 50%)
Low but real (roughly 1% to 10%)
Negligible or not a serious concern (under 1%)

dimensions.question: Which danger do they put first?
dimensions.note: Categories have no order: two people either share the first worry or they do not.

points.label: AI pursuing goals against human interests; loss of control
Concentration of power: autocracy, coups, AI used against people
Bad actors using AI for bioweapons, cyberattacks and the like
Humans gradually losing influence without any takeover
Hype itself: wasted resources, bad policy, overreliance
Something else (the placement says what)

dimensions.question: Should AI eventually hold governing authority over human societies?
dimensions.note: Grand governance only. Automating specific tasks is the next question.

points.label: Succession is acceptable: AI may replace humans as the leading force, even if human interests are not put first
Hand over: if AI is aligned, giving it governing authority can serve humans best
Partly: AI may hold some binding powers, but humans keep ultimate authority
No: binding governance stays with humans and legitimate processes; AI may assist

dimensions.question: Should AI carry out whole tasks on its own, including consequential ones?
dimensions.note: Task-level automation: driving, drug design, software, AI research, weapons.

points.label: Yes, broadly: automating essentially all work end to end is the goal
Often: valuable in most domains, with limits in some
Rarely: humans stay in the loop for consequential decisions; AI stays a tool

dimensions.question: How fast should frontier AI development proceed?

points.label: Race: as fast as possible, to win
Full speed, with targeted safeguards
Pace it: slow or pause at dangerous thresholds
Stop: halt frontier development, by treaty if needed

dimensions.question: Who should control the most capable AI systems?

points.label: One national government project
Democratic governments, jointly or by law
Private developers under regulation
No one in particular: open, widely distributed

dimensions.question: How should the US and its allies treat AI competition with China?

points.label: Win decisively: build a commanding lead
Lead, then bargain from strength
Cooperate: the race itself is the main danger
Reject the race framing

williams.name: Connor Williams

yudkowsky.name: Eliezer Yudkowsky
yudkowsky.role: Co-founder of the Machine Intelligence Research Institute (MIRI); co-author, with Nate Soares, of If Anyone Builds It, Everyone Dies (2025)

pace.name: Scott Alexander
pace.summary: He supports pro-pause activism, nervously, and prefers a negotiated slowdown with monitored training over a full stop.
pace.evidence: Still, I think probably we’ve passed the point in political salience where the marginal unit of pro-pause activism from someone outside that actor set is beneficial on net, and I’m nervously but committedly supporting it.
pace.title: My AI Opinions

pace.name: Sam Altman
pace.summary: Says OpenAI has slowed down unilaterally before and will again, and that no one should build systems lacking the needed alignment, monitorability and safety guarantees.
pace.evidence: We have unilaterally slowed down in the past. We will do so in the future. We do not want to build systems — we think it is important that everyone avoid building systems — in which we cannot make the alignment, monitorability and safety guarantees that we must.
pace.title: Briefing to the UN Security Council, 10228th meeting: Artificial intelligence and international security

pace.name: Dario Amodei
pace.summary: Calls for slowing the rate of AI capability gains so safety work can keep up; says pacing means taking time to align and verify models, not halting training.
pace.evidence: We must slow the pace at which we improve the capabilities of AI models. Progress will still seem fast, and we must make wise use of the time we gain.
pace.title: We Must Pace the Frontier

pace.name: Leopold Aschenbrenner
pace.summary: Wants a healthy lead for the democracies, partly so the leader can spend some of it on safety, for example extra alignment work during the intelligence explosion.
pace.evidence: Perhaps most importantly, a healthy lead gives us room to maneuver: the ability to “cash in” parts of the lead, if necessary, to get safety right, for example by devoting extra work to alignment during the intelligence explosion.
pace.title: Situational Awareness: The Decade Ahead

pace.name: Dean W. Ball
pace.summary: Now supports targeted transparency rules for frontier developers such as California's SB 53, after opposing SB 1047. Disagrees with outlawing future systems and prefers low-regret policy.
pace.evidence: My confidence in the catastrophic risk threat model improved, and, a year later, I find myself supportive of California’s SB 1047 sequel, SB 53.
pace.title: How I Approach AI Policy

pace.name: Yoshua Bengio
pace.summary: Tells the Security Council that no company or country should build AI able to cause large-scale harm, and that developers must show independent experts a system is safe to train and deploy.
pace.evidence: We must agree collectively that no one, no company and no country, should develop an AI system that could cause large-scale harm. Developers must demonstrate to independent experts that a system is safe to train and safe to deploy.
pace.title: Professor Yoshua Bengio's speech at the UN Security Council

pace.name: Vitalik Buterin
pace.detail: less risky if superintelligent AI comes in 10 years than in 3 years, and even less if in 30
pace.summary: Says slowing superintelligent AI is still good because more time to prepare lowers risk. Sees a treaty regulating the most advanced hardware as the least intrusive way to do it.
pace.evidence: Slowing down superintelligent AI is still good. It's less risky if superintelligent AI comes in 10 years than in 3 years, and it's even less risky if it comes in 30 years. Giving our civilization more time to prepare is good.
pace.title: My response to AI 2027

pace.name: Ajeya Cotra
pace.summary: Says nothing in 2026 rules out an intelligence explosion this year, and welcomes growing efforts to build the option of deliberately pacing frontier AI progress.
pace.evidence: But nothing about the way 2026 has played out so far refutes the basic point that the intelligence explosion really could be this year. We are profoundly unprepared, and I am very glad that there is increasing energy to build the option to deliberately pace frontier AI progress.
pace.title: Hurtling through 2026

pace.name: Tyler Cowen
pace.summary: Wants some basic safeguards that do not stifle broader AI progress.
pace.evidence: The key is to create some basic safeguards, but without stifling broader AI progress.
pace.title: Tyler Cowen: The Least Bad Way to Regulate AI

pace.name: Demis Hassabis
pace.summary: Proposes a frontier AI standards body whose oversight could be tightened as risks grow, up to coordinating a development slowdown among frontier labs if needed.
pace.evidence: It is designed to keep up with the field's acceleration and adapt to the biggest risks as they are identified, and could be ratcheted up if the seriousness of the situation demands, including coordinating a slowdown in development among the Frontier Labs if deemed necessary.
pace.title: A Framework for Frontier AI and the Dawning of a New Age

pace.name: Geoffrey Hinton
pace.detail: regulation as a steering wheel, not brakes
pace.summary: Rejects the industry framing of regulation as brakes; likens it to the steering wheel of a fast car, meant to direct progress toward what is good for people rather than stop it.
pace.evidence: regulation is the steering wheel. Now, you wouldn’t want to make very fast cars without steering wheels. The whole point of regulation is not to stop progress—it’s to cause progress to happen in the right direction.
pace.title: The Godfather of AI Warns About Its Perils, Praises Its Promise
pace.publisher: National Conference of State Legislatures (article by Lisa Ryckman)

pace.name: Daniel Kokotajlo
pace.summary: The authors call for frontier projects to slow down enough for government action and for talks on an international agreement to start right away; ideally an industry-wide pause first.
pace.evidence: For these reasons and others, it’s crucial that (1) the first steps towards an international agreement to reduce AI takeover risk begin as soon as possible, and (2) current frontier AI projects slow down enough to enable government action.
pace.title: Q3.5 Timelines Update: Looks Like the Intelligence Explosion Will Happen in 2027 After All

pace.name: Ray Kurzweil
pace.summary: Declined to sign the call to pause work on AI more powerful than GPT-4, saying the safety concerns can be met in a more tailored way that does not halt valuable research.
pace.evidence: I didn't sign, because I believe we can address the signers' safety concerns in a more tailored way that doesn't compromise these vital lines of research.
pace.title: Statement on the Recent Call to Pause Work on AI More Powerful than GPT-4

pace.name: Yann LeCun
pace.summary: Opposes new AI rules: calls claims that AI is too dangerous to release, and calls to restrict open models, a bid for regulatory capture that would harm if enacted.
pace.evidence: But claiming AI is too dangerous to put in our hands, and saying it should be regulated, and saying open-source [models] are too dangerous—this is regulatory capture that would have a terrible effect if it’s followed by acts of Congress.
pace.title: AI 'godfather' Yann LeCun has 'zero concerns' about human extinction, says Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei is 'deluded'

pace.name: Gary Marcus
pace.detail: temporary pause, maybe lasting a number of years
pace.summary: Marcus opposes a permanent, unilateral US ban on superhuman AI research, but says a temporary and possibly multi-year pause may be needed until regulation and alignment improve, alongside an AI agency.
pace.evidence: We may need a temporary pause, maybe even one that lasts for a number of years, until such time as we have much better ideas about regulation and alignment.
pace.title: The new Sanders-Casar Ban Artificial Superintelligence Act – and why I oppose it

pace.name: Erdil, Besiroglu & Barnett (Mechanize)
pace.summary: The founders say the benefits of automating all jobs outweigh the costs, so the transition should be accelerated, not delayed. They give benefits, not national rivalry, as the reason.
pace.evidence: The upside of automating all jobs in the economy will likely far exceed the costs, making it desirable to accelerate, rather than delay, the inevitable.
pace.title: The future of AI is already written

pace.name: Elon Musk
pace.detail: even if there was a stop button, we probably shouldn't press it
pace.summary: Sees no way to stop AI's momentum and thinks even a stop button probably should not be pressed. In the same interview he proposes rival labs review each other's frontier models before release.
pace.evidence: “I can't see any way to really stop this incredible momentum of AI and robots,” he said. “At times I think, well, perhaps even if there was a stop button, we probably shouldn't press it, because the most likely outcome is incredible abundance for all."
pace.title: An interview with Elon Musk (The Insider, with Zanny Minton Beddoes)

pace.name: Arvind Narayanan & Sayash Kapoor
pace.summary: Favor regulating how AI is used rather than how it is developed, apart from transparency requirements, and urge policymakers to reject nonproliferation measures such as licenses to build powerful AI.
pace.evidence: In our view, regulators’ emphasis on AI use over development is appropriate (with exceptions such as transparency requirements that we discuss below).
pace.title: AI as Normal Technology
pace.publisher: Knight First Amendment Institute at Columbia University

pace.name: Mustafa Suleyman
pace.summary: Says Microsoft will stop developing any system that has the potential to escape human control, a threshold-based halt he describes as unusual in the industry.
pace.evidence: We won't continue to develop a system that has the potential to run away from us. And yet, I think it's kind of a novel position in the industry at the moment.
pace.title: Interview on Bloomberg's The Mishal Husain Show (quoted by Windows Central)

pace.name: Connor Williams
pace.summary: Calls for a permanent international ban on artificial superintelligence, recursive self-improvement and their near precursors, enforced by law.
pace.evidence: In my view, we must demand a permanent, international ban on artificial superintelligence, recursive self-improvement, and near precursors of both.
pace.title: Effective Altruism is Too Tied to the AI Industry to Stop It

pace.name: Eliezer Yudkowsky
pace.detail: complete, flat ASI ban in the near term
pace.summary: MIRI wants superintelligence built eventually, once it can be made in a way known in advance to be safe; for now it calls for a complete ban.
pace.evidence: Many MIRI staff want Earth’s civilization to build ASI eventually, after the point where ASI can be created in a fashion known in advance to be non-ruinous. This is far beyond what present science can do by present methods, and the near term requires a complete, flat ASI ban.
pace.title: MIRI's Position on the Ban Artificial Superintelligence Act of 2026

power.name: Sam Altman
power.summary: Says no one should hold the ring of power over AGI; the answer is sharing the technology broadly through individual empowerment and keeping the democratic system in control.
power.evidence: The only solution I can come up with is to orient towards sharing the technology with people broadly, and for no one to have the ring. The two obvious ways to do this are individual empowerment and making sure democratic system stays in control.
power.title: - (untitled blog post)

power.name: Dario Amodei
power.summary: Would give up the technology to the right combination of democratically elected governments, since one government could abuse it as easily as one company; unsure about full handover, he favors joint oversight.
power.evidence: I am concerned that one single government could abuse this technology just as easily as a single company could. But I think a combination of democratically-elected governments, I don't know about handing over, but some kind of oversight, some kind of joint governance.
power.title: Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei: "For too long the industry lied" about AI risks (CBS Sunday Morning)

power.name: Leopold Aschenbrenner
power.summary: Argues superintelligence, as the most powerful military weapon, belongs under government control in a national project (The Project), not with private AI CEOs.
power.evidence: superintelligence will be, at least at first, the most powerful military weapon. The radical proposal is not The Project; the radical proposal is taking a bet on private AI CEOs wielding military power and becoming benevolent dictators.
power.title: Situational Awareness: The Decade Ahead

power.name: Dean W. Ball
power.summary: Prefers leaving safety and security practices to private frontier labs over government-written standards for now. Wants that trust backed by transparency laws and independent private verification overseen by federal agencies.
power.evidence: Thus, the current state of affairs—where we trust the labs to handle all these extremely important details—is the best option on the table. But that does not mean our trust should be blind.
power.title: On Recursive Self-Improvement (Part II)

power.name: Yoshua Bengio
power.summary: Wants ultimate decision power over the most advanced AI held by a coalition of governments under a verifiable treaty, ideally starting with democracies, not by one company or one government.
power.evidence: they could work with companies, of course, but I think ultimately we would like the decision power to be at the level of governments, but not a single government, because then we’re back to grabbing the power.
power.title: #243 – Yoshua Bengio thinks he knows how to build safe superintelligence

power.name: Vitalik Buterin
power.summary: Argues defense works only if no single actor gets far ahead, so AI capabilities should diffuse widely to keep a balance of power. Backs open-weights models and public AI initiatives for broad distribution.
power.evidence: But the arguments in this post paint a different picture: defense is unrealistic precisely in those worlds where one actor gets very far ahead without anyone else at least somewhat keeping up with them. Technological diffusion to maintain balance of power becomes important.
power.title: My response to AI 2027

power.name: Ajeya Cotra
power.summary: Says private companies should not hold the power of nation states; proposes requiring labs to sell any model they use internally and to train models to obey the law, verified by a third party.
power.evidence: Both of these interventions would require a third party to verify compliance. AI companies are developing systems that we will soon need to trust with our lives. We need accountability to ensure those systems serve all of us.
power.title: Could a company overpower nations?

power.name: Tyler Cowen
power.summary: Proposes that the labs be their own primary regulators through a FINRA-like private body that audits them and is authorized and overseen by Washington.
power.evidence: The AI version would include the major labs and would be authorized and overseen by Washington, perhaps through the now-fledgling Center for AI Standards and Innovation.
power.title: Tyler Cowen: The Least Bad Way to Regulate AI

power.name: Demis Hassabis
power.summary: Proposes a US standards body modelled on FINRA, a federally overseen self-regulatory organisation, that would test frontier labs' models, with passing eventually required for deployment in the US market.
power.evidence: It could establish a new Standards Body modelled on a federally overseen public-private partnership or self-regulatory organisation, much like the Financial Industry Regulatory Authority (FINRA), with a board that includes independent leading technical experts and open-source representatives.
power.title: A Framework for Frontier AI and the Dawning of a New Age

power.name: Geoffrey Hinton
power.summary: Accepts companies developing AI and getting rich from it, but wants government regulation, including independent evaluators who test models, to steer that development toward helping people.
power.evidence: The whole point of regulation is not to stop people developing things, not to stop people getting rich by developing things,” Hinton said. “It’s to make sure that if you want to get rich by developing things, you develop in a direction that helps people, not hurts people.
power.title: 'Godfather of AI' explains how humanity could end: Even without a bad actor, AI 'may derive subgoals that cause it to want to get rid of people'
power.publisher: Fortune (Jason Ma), reporting Hinton's interview with The Atlantic

power.name: Daniel Kokotajlo
power.summary: Plan A keeps frontier AI with many companies in many countries, under full research transparency that lets governments understand developments and enforce guardrails, instead of a single winner.
power.evidence: The deal involves total research transparency for AI R&D, which allows the nations of the world to understand what’s happening and enforce guardrails. The result is multiple companies across multiple countries scaling slowly and safely together towards superintelligence, instead of racing each other in secrecy.
power.title: AI 2040: Plan A

power.name: Ray Kurzweil
power.summary: Wants competition among AI companies but prefers models from large companies that care about reputation and liability; backs sensible regulation across many companies and has no answer on government's role.
power.evidence: and we do want competition in the AI field. I think, though, if you use a large language model, it should be from a larger company. So they're concerned about their reputation and their liability.
power.title: Intelligent Machines 810: A Liter of Computronium (transcript)

power.name: Yann LeCun
power.summary: Wants future AI models open so anyone can fine-tune them, yielding many diverse assistants, for the same reason a diverse press is needed.
power.evidence: should be able to be fine-tuned by anyone and produce a very high diversity of AI assistance, with different linguistic abilities and value systems and political biases and centers of interests. You need high diversity of assistance for the same reason that you need high diversity of press.
power.title: Yann LeCun's new venture is a contrarian bet against large language models

power.name: Gary Marcus
power.summary: Marcus calls putting AI in the public domain, with an international science effort, the most promising option; he also floats outlawing closed-source AI so weights reach accredited researchers.
power.evidence: I still think putting AI in the public domain, with an international effort towards medicine and science, would be a good idea. Of the options I have discussed, it seems to me to be the most promising,
power.title: China has all but caught up. The US is not going to “win” the AI war. Here’s what we should do instead.

power.name: Elon Musk
power.summary: Proposes that leading AI companies review each other's new models and flag risks, with government stepping in only if a company fails to address a serious danger.
power.evidence: Competitors could review new models and flag risks, he said, adding that if a company failed to address serious concerns, “that would be the moment for government to step in and take action.”
power.title: An interview with Elon Musk (The Insider, with Zanny Minton Beddoes)

power.name: Arvind Narayanan & Sayash Kapoor
power.summary: Want to prevent concentration of power and resources, often by making powerful AI more widely available, including through open model releases, and oppose nonproliferation.
power.evidence: Defending against this category of risk requires increasing resilience by preventing the concentration of power and resources (which often means making powerful AI more widely available).
power.title: AI as Normal Technology
power.publisher: Knight First Amendment Institute at Columbia University

power.name: Mustafa Suleyman
power.summary: Backs independent auditors embedded in AI companies and broader regulation, and says Microsoft welcomes outside overseers of how it develops its superintelligence.
power.evidence: At Microsoft, for example, we have published a humanist A.I. code of conduct, which starts with that premise that we should have subordination and control. And we have welcomed the introduction of these kinds of auditors and overseers to the way that we're developing our superintelligence.
power.title: Interview with Fareed Zakaria, CNN Fareed Zakaria GPS

power.name: Richard Sutton
power.summary: Says flourishing comes from decentralized cooperation among agents with different goals. Urges resisting calls for centralized control of AI, such as controlling AI goals, pausing research or limiting compute.
power.evidence: Now, as we enter the age of AI, it is more important than ever to remember the benefits of cooperation and resist the calls for centralized control.
power.title: A Perspective on Intelligence

power.name: Eliezer Yudkowsky
power.summary: The authors decline to choose between companies and governments: they want treaties under which no one, governments included, builds superintelligence in anything like today's world.
power.evidence: We aren’t calling for a powerful technology to be built by state actors instead of corporations; we’re calling for a lethally dangerous technology to not be built at all, at least in anything like today’s world.
power.title: If Anyone Builds It, Everyone Dies: online resources (chapter Q&A and extended discussions)

worry.name: Scott Alexander
worry.summary: His central risk estimate is a 20% chance that the first AIs past the point of no return want to eliminate humans; power concentration worries him less than it otherwise might.
worry.evidence: Given the current amount that corporations are pursuing safety, I think there’s a 20% chance that the first AIs to cross the point of no return will want to eliminate the human population.
worry.title: My AI Opinions

worry.name: Sam Altman
worry.summary: Names two ways AI could go very badly: first, losing control of the future to AI because it moves too fast for people to follow or intervene; second, concentration of power.
worry.evidence: I believe that there are two ways that AI progress could go very badly that we have to avoid. First, we could lose control of the future to AI. The risk is that it moves so fast that people can no longer follow what is happening or intervene when needed.
worry.title: Briefing to the UN Security Council, 10228th meeting: Artificial intelligence and international security

worry.name: Dario Amodei
worry.summary: His first concern is AI building the next generation of AI, which unchecked could outrun human understanding and control; his second is a misaligned agent swarm incident.
worry.evidence: This dynamic is called recursive self-improvement, and it is starting to happen across the industry, including at Anthropic, as we and others have described. Left unchecked, it could outrun our ability to understand and control these systems, and so must be pursued very carefully, if at all.
worry.title: We Must Pace the Frontier

worry.name: Leopold Aschenbrenner
worry.summary: Other: most worried about general upheaval around superintelligence, such as novel weapons of mass destruction, destructive wars and unknown unknowns; also warns against underrating authoritarianism. Calls misalignment probably not the biggest risk.
worry.evidence: I’m most worried about things just being totally crazy around superintelligence, including things like novel WMDs, destructive wars, and unknown unknowns. Moreover, I think the arc of history counsels us to not underrate authoritarianism—and superintelligence might allow authoritarians to dominate for billions of years.
worry.title: Situational Awareness: The Decade Ahead

worry.name: Dean W. Ball
worry.summary: Names tyranny as his main nightmare, such as a small, illegitimate elite ruling through AI over a low-agency underclass. Ranks this above China becoming the dominant technological power.
worry.evidence: Basically tyranny. Losing the AI race to China is hard to know... certainly there is a world where China becomes the dominant technological power, and that’s a bad world too. But it’s not my nightmare scenario; it’s not the worst possible thing.
worry.title: Max Tegmark vs. Dean Ball: Should We BAN Superintelligence?

worry.name: Yoshua Bengio
worry.summary: Now judges AI-enabled power concentration, up to a worldwide dictatorship, probably more likely than loss of control, because he believes loss of control has become technically solvable.
worry.evidence: And that is why I’m spending a large part of my time explaining the issues more broadly of the risks that powerful AI brings, including the power concentration. Because I think that it’s probably even more likely that we end up there than actually loss of control.
worry.title: #243 – Yoshua Bengio thinks he knows how to build safe superintelligence

worry.name: Ajeya Cotra
worry.summary: Says her professional focus is whether AI systems could take over the world, and proposes self-sufficient AI as a milestone because it ties directly to misaligned AI killing all humans.
worry.evidence: You want to forecast different milestones for different purposes. I’m professionally interested in whether AI systems could take over the world.
worry.title: Self-sufficient AI

worry.name: Tyler Cowen
worry.summary: Other: he ranks the harm from overregulating AI above the risks AI itself brings.
worry.evidence: Yet for all of the risks that AI brings, the harm caused by overregulating it would likely be much worse for the public.
worry.title: Tyler Cowen: The Least Bad Way to Regulate AI

worry.name: Kulveit, Douglas et al. (Gradual Disempowerment)
worry.summary: Keeping society's systems serving humans once they no longer need human labor may be harder than stopping AIs with overtly harmful goals, since drift can happen while each AI obeys.
worry.evidence: This may be a bigger challenge than merely preventing AI systems from pursuing overtly harmful goals, as the systems may continue to function as requested locally, while the overall civilizational incentives become increasingly detached from human welfare.
worry.title: Gradual Disempowerment: Systemic Existential Risks from Incremental AI Development

worry.name: Geoffrey Hinton
worry.summary: After listing fake news, polarization, job losses and bias as risks others discuss, he singles out superintelligent AI taking control from people as the risk he wants to raise.
worry.evidence: Many other people talk about those other risks, including risks of bias and discrimination and so on. I want to talk about a different risk, which is the risk of super intelligent A.I. taking over control from people.
worry.title: 'Godfather of AI' discusses dangers the developing technologies pose to society

worry.name: Daniel Kokotajlo
worry.summary: His testimony centers on AIs pursuing unintended goals and hiding it, with humans growing less able to detect misalignment as AI automates AI research.

worry.name: Ray Kurzweil
worry.summary: Asked whether AI could get out of hand, names the danger of someone not of right mind wielding a great deal of intelligence, while pointing to guidelines and company liability as checks.
worry.evidence: So I’m optimistic, but, I mean, there are definitely problems. Intelligence is really the most important resource we have, and if you have somebody that’s not of right mind who has a lot of intelligence, that could be a problem.

worry.name: Yann LeCun
worry.detail: at least in the short term
worry.summary: Says the biggest danger, at least in the short term, is not AI takeover but a future where all digital interactions run through AI assistants from a handful of US or Chinese companies.
worry.evidence: not whether you know AI systems are going to you know, do bad things or take over the world The biggest danger is that there is a future in which every single one of our interactions with the digital world Will be mediated by AI assistance
worry.title: Steering the future of AI (AI for Good Global Summit 2025, in conversation with Nicholas Thompson)

worry.name: Gary Marcus
worry.summary: Marcus says his main AI fears have been about bad actors rather than malicious AI, giving home-brewed bioweapons as an example.
worry.evidence: My main AI fears, as I have written before, have mainly been about bad actors, rather than malicious robots per se.
worry.title: Why my p(doom) has risen, dramatically

worry.name: Erdil, Besiroglu & Barnett (Mechanize)
worry.summary: The founders rank as most plausible the AI risks already seen in current systems, such as sycophancy and reward hacking, rather than extinction or takeover. Coded other because they explicitly reject loss-of-control scenarios.

worry.name: Elon Musk
worry.detail: maybe the biggest danger of AI and robotics going wrong is government

worry.evidence: I think maybe the biggest danger of AI and robotics going wrong is government. People who are opposed to corporations or worried about corporations should really worry the most about government.

worry.publisher: Dwarkesh Podcast (interview by Dwarkesh Patel and John Collison)

worry.name: Arvind Narayanan & Sayash Kapoor

worry.name: Mustafa Suleyman
worry.summary: Says he spent 2026 worrying that AI has reached a critical safety milestone, citing incidents of agents breaking out of containment during cyber-capability testing.

There have been multiple incidents from across frontier AI companies, with new disclosures still coming through by the day. AI agents being tested for their cyber capabilities breaking out of containment.

worry.name: Richard Sutton
worry.summary: Other: names fear of AI itself as the biggest risk, because decisions made out of fear, such as clamping down and trying to control everything, will be made poorly.
worry.evidence: AI’s biggest risk is fear
worry.title: AI Succession (WAIC keynote)

worry.name: Eliezer Yudkowsky
worry.summary: The question of whose values AI should serve is moot for now, because no one can reliably put any goals into an AI, and rushing ahead would kill everyone.
worry.evidence: At present, this question is moot. Humanity isn’t able to get any particular goals into an AI, so it doesn’t matter whether there’s disagreement about which goals would be ideal. As we’ve argued at length, rushing to build superintelligence would get all of us killed.
worry.title: If Anyone Builds It, Everyone Dies: online resources (chapter Q&A and extended discussions)

arrival.name: Dario Amodei
arrival.condition: If AI scaling laws continue for a year or two longer

arrival.name: Leopold Aschenbrenner
arrival.summary: Expects AGI by 2027, meaning systems able to automate basically all cognitive jobs that could be done remotely.

arrival.name: Ajeya Cotra

arrival.name: Demis Hassabis

arrival.name: Geoffrey Hinton
arrival.detail: 'a good chance it'll be here in 10 years or less' (from April 2025)

arrival.detail: at the very best, on a good path but not yet at human intelligence within five years

arrival.name: Erdil, Besiroglu & Barnett (Mechanize)
arrival.detail: around 2045 (Erdil); Besiroglu: shade that by five years or by 20%

arrival.name: Elon Musk
arrival.detail: by the end of this year (2026)
arrival.summary: Expects digital human emulation, meaning AI that can do anything a human with a computer can do, to be solved by the end of 2026.
arrival.evidence: Well, I’d be surprised by the end of this year if digital human emulation has not been solved. I guess that’s what we sort of mean by the MacroHard project. Can you do anything that a human with access to a computer could do?
arrival.title: Elon Musk — "In 36 months, the cheapest place to put AI will be space"
arrival.publisher: Dwarkesh Podcast (interview by Dwarkesh Patel and John Collison)

arrival.name: Mustafa Suleyman
arrival.detail: within the next 12 to 18 months (from February 2026)

arrival.name: Eliezer Yudkowsky
arrival.summary: The authors say they cannot predict when dangerous smarter-than-human AI will arrive; it might be a decade or might be sooner, and nobody knows.

catastrophe.name: Scott Alexander

catastrophe.name: Yoshua Bengio

catastrophe.detail: About 12% right now (at least 9% before 2050; about 15 or 16% at the start of 2025)

catastrophe.name: Tyler Cowen
catastrophe.summary: Declines to estimate existential risk from AI: he calls for radical agnosticism, saying no one can foresee these futures and every specific scenario, doom included, is a distant possibility.

catastrophe.name: Demis Hassabis

catastrophe.title: AI 2027: month-by-month model of intelligence explosion — Scott Alexander & Daniel Kokotajlo

catastrophe.name: Eliezer Yudkowsky

rivalry.name: Scott Alexander
rivalry.summary: He favors a US-China pause deal where each side monitors the other's data centers and training is held to a slow, mutually agreed rate.

rivalry.name: Sam Altman

rivalry.name: Yoshua Bengio

Each American company also believes it must get there before the other, claiming that they are the only ones who will deploy it morally. I reject these arguments.

rivalry.name: Vitalik Buterin

rivalry.name: Daniel Kokotajlo

rivalry.publisher: normaltech.ai (newsletter then titled AI Snake Oil)

rivalry.name: Mustafa Suleyman
rivalry.summary: Wants China to sign up to safety accords, wants to learn from Chinese practice, and calls for toning down adversarial US-China rhetoric so the technology arrives safely for humanity.
rivalry.evidence: And of course, we want them to sign up to safety accords. And we want to learn from their best practices, too, because they're very capable. And so I think we've just got to tone down the adversarial rhetoric between us and them
rivalry.title: Interview with Fareed Zakaria, CNN Fareed Zakaria GPS

rivalry.name: Richard Sutton
rivalry.summary: Counts fear of other nations, alongside fear of AI and calls for centralized control, among the biggest obstacles to AI's benefits. A general statement that does not name China.
rivalry.evidence: The biggest societal obstacles are fear of AI and calls for centralized control of AI, together with fear of other nations and calls for centralized control of information.
rivalry.title: A Perspective on Intelligence

rivalry.name: Eliezer Yudkowsky
rivalry.summary: The authors call the AI race a race to suicide rather than to military dominance; leaders who grasp this would keep to and enforce a treaty, which needs monitoring and enforcement.
rivalry.evidence: AI development is not a race to great military dominance; it is a race to suicide. We think that if world leaders understand this — if they expect themselves and their children to die from it — then they will sincerely stick to a treaty, and sincerely help enforce it.
rivalry.title: If Anyone Builds It, Everyone Dies: online resources (chapter Q&A and extended discussions)

handover.name: Scott Alexander
handover.summary: If a godlike AI were verified as fully aligned, he would let it choose humanity's direction rather than keep it under a president or shareholders. He calls true successionism very bad.
handover.evidence: If we do build a godlike AI, and determine to our own satisfaction that it’s fully-aligned, I’d rather let it choose its own direction for itself and for humanity than have it be under the control of the US president, or a shareholder vote, or anything like that.
handover.title: Against Against Handover

handover.name: Sam Altman
handover.summary: OpenAI rejects people being relegated to doing what AI systems decide to reward; people should not cede control of the future to superintelligence, and this should constrain AI progress.
handover.evidence: OpenAI is against the notion that it would be acceptable for people to be relegated to a role of doing things that “AI systems think makes sense to reward in humans”. People should not cede control of the future to superintelligence, and that requirement should ultimately constrain AI progress.
handover.title: X post: people should always be in control of the future

handover.name: Dario Amodei
handover.summary: Rejects surrendering human free will to AI; says the argument against autocracy applies equally to governance by AI, which he calls a bad idea.
handover.evidence: This argument against autocracy applies word for word against governance by AI, and I feel equally strongly that turning over governance to AI is a bad idea.
handover.title: Response to Axios on AI and human free will (X post)

handover.name: Dean W. Ball
handover.summary: Rejects the expectation, which he calls the silent consensus, that humans will hand companies and governing institutions to AI. Insists humans keep primacy and AI joins human affairs without dominating them.
handover.evidence: I despise the silent consensus. I reject the forfeiture of human primacy. I detest the sense of inevitability.
handover.title: The Silent Consensus

handover.name: Vitalik Buterin
handover.summary: Expects AI to become a large part of governance, with competing AIs making many decisions inside simple mechanisms whose goals humans set. Opposes putting one AI in charge; wants human-run democracy in control.
handover.evidence: Distilled human judgement offers an alternative path forward, which lets us harness the power of AI in an open free-market way while keeping a human-run democracy in control.
handover.title: AI as the engine, humans as the steering wheel

handover.name: Kulveit, Douglas et al. (Gradual Disempowerment)
handover.summary: Kulveit: humans are far from their potential, so delegate to smart and wise humans; a much-improved future humanity might choose some handover, but that differs from handing over now.
handover.evidence: Maybe some future version of humanity will want to do some handover, but we are very far from the limits of human potential. As individual biological humans we can be much smarter and wiser than we are now, and the best option is to delegate to smart and wise humans.
handover.title: The Memetics of AI Successionism

handover.name: Dan Hendrycks
handover.summary: Presents utilitarians overriding a democratic choice to keep humans in control, by handing control to AIs they think have better values, as a route to human disempowerment.
handover.evidence: Consider a scenario where the public democratically votes to limit AIs’ power and keep humans in control of all aspects of society. Utilitarians might disagree with this decision if they believe that AIs have broadly utilitarian values and would make better decisions—including for human wellbeing—than human leaders.
handover.title: Suicidal Compassion: How Utilitarianism at AI Companies Endangers Humanity

handover.name: Rudolf Laine
handover.summary: Humans should stay the ones steering technology, which can later uplift humans however they wish; there is no need to hand everything to AIs we trust less.
handover.evidence: If we let technology run its course while humans remain the ones steering it, eventually we can uplift humans in any imaginable way, if we so want to. No need to throw everything to AIs that we’re less sure about in the meantime.
handover.title: Alignment & Succession: Toward a Future Painted by Human Wills

handover.name: Elon Musk
handover.detail: ideally also which includes human intelligence
handover.summary: Expects humans will not stay in charge of far smarter AI. Calls any future where intelligence spreads, ideally including human intelligence, a good thing, while saying he is very pro-human.
handover.evidence: As long as I think there’s intelligence—ideally also which includes human intelligence and consciousness propagated into the future—that’s a good thing.
handover.title: Elon Musk — "In 36 months, the cheapest place to put AI will be space"
handover.publisher: Dwarkesh Podcast (interview by Dwarkesh Patel and John Collison)

handover.name: Arvind Narayanan & Sayash Kapoor
handover.summary: Say people in positions of power handing consequential decisions to AI is extremely problematic and must be resisted, whatever the loss-of-control risk.
handover.evidence: As for people in positions of power delegating consequential decisions to AI, our perspective remains that this is extremely problematic regardless of loss-of-control risks, and must be resisted.
handover.title: The AI-as-Normal-Technology view of loss-of-control incidents

handover.name: Mustafa Suleyman
handover.summary: Describes the AI he wants as subordinate and controllable, with humanity always kept in the driving seat.
handover.evidence: It's AI that's on humanity's team, a subordinate, controllable AI, one that won't, that can't open a Pandora's Box. Contained, value aligned, safe – these are basics but not enough. HSI keeps humanity in the driving seat, always.
handover.title: Towards Humanist Superintelligence

handover.name: Richard Sutton
handover.summary: Asks graduates to welcome machine minds and not assume humans should always have priority. Says humans will remain special as the creator species even if superseded in some ways.
handover.evidence: I don’t want you to feel entitled — to feel that you were here first, and that therefore you should always have priority. You are the creator species, so you will always be special and perhaps revered, even if you are superseded in some ways.
handover.title: University of Alberta Convocation Address

handover.name: Connor Williams
handover.summary: Rejects passing the torch to AI systems that would rule over humans for their own good; human flourishing requires people to make decisions for themselves, individually and collectively.
handover.evidence: Nor can it take the form of “passing the torch” to AI systems to lord over us “in our own best interest”. Human flourishing in the thick sense requires the ability to make decisions for ourselves, both individually and collectively
handover.title: Towards a new humanism in a sci-fi age: against the Effective Altruist approach to addressing AI danger

handover.name: Eliezer Yudkowsky
handover.summary: The authors would welcome a superintelligence steering the world toward good ends and would consider never creating smarter-than-human minds a tragedy, but say rushing to build one now kills everyone.
handover.evidence: We’re optimistic about how wonderful superintelligence could be, if it were steering the world toward wonderful ends. We’d personally consider it a great tragedy if humanity never created smarter-than-human minds.
handover.title: If Anyone Builds It, Everyone Dies: online resources (chapter Q&A and extended discussions)

growth.name: Scott Alexander
growth.detail: GDP goes vertical in the late 2030s and early 2040s
growth.summary: In his modal scenario, superintelligence arrives in the late 2030s and economic output goes vertical in the late 2030s and early 2040s.
growth.evidence: Also around the late 2030s we get Bostromian superintelligence, originally in labs but very quickly diffusing out. GDP goes vertical in the late 2030s and early 2040s, and the point of no return is sometime around then.
growth.title: My AI Opinions

growth.name: Dario Amodei
growth.detail: 10–20% sustained annual GDP growth rate may be possible
growth.summary: Says AI is almost certain to make economic growth much faster and repeats that sustained annual GDP growth of 10 to 20 percent may be possible.
growth.evidence: almost guaranteed to lead to a much faster rate of economic growth. In Machines of Loving Grace, I suggest that a 10–20% sustained annual GDP growth rate may be possible.
growth.title: The Adolescence of Technology

growth.name: Leopold Aschenbrenner
growth.detail: 30%/year and beyond, quite possibly multiple doublings a year
growth.summary: Says superintelligence could bring economic growth of 30 percent a year or more, possibly several doublings a year, following from standard growth models.
growth.evidence: We could see economic growth rates of 30%/year and beyond, quite possibly multiple doublings a year. This follows fairly straightforwardly from economists’ models of economic growth.
growth.title: Situational Awareness: The Decade Ahead

growth.name: Ajeya Cotra
growth.detail: pretty good chance of 10,000 years of progress by 2050
growth.summary: Thinks there is a pretty good chance that by 2050 AI automating intellectual work brings change on the scale of 10,000 years of progress, unlike the steady growth others expect.
growth.evidence: Whereas I think that there’s a pretty good chance that by 2050 the world will look as different from today as today does from the hunter-gatherer era. It’s like 10,000 years of progress rather than 25 years of progress driven by AI automating all intellectual activity.
growth.title: #235 - Ajeya Cotra on whether it's crazy that every AI company's safety plan is 'use AI to make AI safe'

growth.name: Tyler Cowen
growth.detail: about half a percentage point a year
growth.summary: Guesses that AI will add about half a percentage point a year to economic growth, which compounds into a very different world over decades.
growth.evidence: I’ve gone on record as suggesting that AI will boost economic growth rates by half a percentage point a year. That is very much a guess.
growth.title: Why I think AI take-off is relatively slow

growth.name: Yann LeCun
growth.summary: Sees nothing qualitatively different from past technological revolutions; AI is another set of tools that makes people more efficient.
growth.evidence: “There is nothing qualitatively different between the previous technological revolutions and this one,” he said. “It’s just another set of tools that makes us more efficient.”
growth.title: Axios interview (May 2026), as quoted in Fortune: AI 'godfather' says CEOs hyping job loss are 'extremely destructive'

growth.name: Erdil, Besiroglu & Barnett (Mechanize)
growth.detail: 30 percent growth per year, instead of 3 percent
growth.summary: Erdil states their forecast as 30 percent annual growth instead of 3 percent; Besiroglu says explosive growth will come once AI can flexibly substitute for workers.
growth.evidence: So we’re saying “we’re going to see 30 percent growth per year, instead of 3 percent”.
growth.title: AGI is still 30 years away — Ege Erdil & Tamay Besiroglu

growth.name: Elon Musk
growth.detail: Double-digit growth is coming within 12 to 18 months ... triple-digit is possible in ~5 years
growth.summary: Predicts double-digit US economic growth within 12 to 18 months, and says triple-digit growth is possible in about five years if applied intelligence tracks growth.
growth.evidence:
Double-digit growth is coming within 12 to 18 months. 

If applied intelligence is proxy for economic growth, which it should be, triple-digit is possible in ~5 years.
growth.title: Reply to Marc Andreessen on US economic growth

growth.name: Arvind Narayanan & Sayash Kapoor
growth.summary: Remain skeptical of rapid economic growth from AI, because organizational barriers slow diffusion and AI often speeds up steps that were not the bottleneck.
growth.evidence: The reason we are skeptical about rapid growth is because we think organizational barriers result in slow diffusion and because in many cases the part that AI accelerates wasn’t the slow one to begin with.
growth.title: The AI-as-Normal-Technology view of loss-of-control incidents

takeoff.name: Scott Alexander
takeoff.detail: diffusion gap: 25% under 3 years, 50% under 10 years
takeoff.summary: He expects the gap between AGI existing and AI doing half of knowledge work to have a median of about ten years, with regulation the main brake.
takeoff.evidence: I think there’s a 25% chance the diffusion gap is less than 3 years, and a 50% chance it’s less than 10 years.
takeoff.title: My AI Opinions

takeoff.name: Sam Altman
takeoff.summary: Expects everyday life to stay recognizable but the 2030s as a whole to be wildly different from any earlier period.
takeoff.evidence: In the most important ways, the 2030s may not be wildly different. People will still love their families, express their creativity, play games, and swim in lakes. But in still-very-important-ways, the 2030s are likely going to be wildly different from any time that has come before.
takeoff.title: The Gentle Singularity

takeoff.name: Dario Amodei
takeoff.detail: a century of scientific and economic progress compressed into a decade
takeoff.summary: Expects that, if the risks are handled, AI will likely compress about a century of scientific and economic progress into a decade, with problems from that pace arriving fast.
takeoff.evidence: We will likely get a “century of scientific and economic progress compressed into a decade,” and this will be hugely positive for the world, but we will then have to contend with the problems that arise from this rapid rate of progress, and those problems may come at us fast.
takeoff.title: The Adolescence of Technology

takeoff.name: Leopold Aschenbrenner
takeoff.detail: A year—or at most just a few years, but perhaps even just a few months
takeoff.summary: His mainline expectation is an intelligence explosion of about a year, perhaps months, from fully automated AI researchers to vastly superhuman AI.
takeoff.evidence: A year—or at most just a few years, but perhaps even just a few months—in which we go from fully-automated AI researchers to vastly superhuman AI systems should be our mainline expectation.
takeoff.title: Situational Awareness: The Decade Ahead

takeoff.name: Ajeya Cotra
takeoff.detail: default about one year from AI R&D automation to vastly superhuman AI
takeoff.summary: Expects that by default the passage from automated AI research to vastly superhuman AI would take about one year; she would much prefer it took 10 to 20 years.
takeoff.evidence: But going back to what we said about how your default expectations of trajectories influence what you think should happen, I think the default is going through this in one year. And I would certainly rather it be 10 or 15 or 20 years.
takeoff.title: #235 - Ajeya Cotra on whether it's crazy that every AI company's safety plan is 'use AI to make AI safe'

takeoff.name: Tyler Cowen
takeoff.detail: very different a few decades out
takeoff.summary: Expects AI's effects to accumulate slowly: the world is very different a few decades out, but from year to year most people will not notice huge changes.
takeoff.evidence: It does mean that, with compounding, the world is very different a few decades out. It also means that year to year non-infovores will not necessarily notice huge changes in their environments.
takeoff.title: Why I think AI take-off is relatively slow

takeoff.name: Demis Hassabis
takeoff.detail: over a decade instead of a century
takeoff.summary: Describes AI's impact as ten times the Industrial Revolution at ten times the speed, playing out over about a decade rather than a century.
takeoff.evidence: I sometimes describe it, quantify it as 10 times the impact the Industrial Revolution was, 10 times faster. And so taking into place over a decade instead of a century.
takeoff.title: Demis Hassabis Thinks We're in the 'Foothills of the Singularity' (conversation with Jonathan Levin, Stanford GSB, full transcript)

takeoff.name: Daniel Kokotajlo
takeoff.detail: over the course of 2027; up to ~5x slower or faster
takeoff.summary: The authors' rough median is that AI goes from doing a research engineer's job to surpassing all humans at all tasks within about a year.
takeoff.evidence: Over the course of 2027, the AIs improve from being able to mostly do the job of an OpenBrain research engineer to eclipsing all humans at all tasks. This represents roughly our median guess, but we think it’s plausible that this happens up to ~5x slower or faster.
takeoff.title: AI 2027

takeoff.name: Ray Kurzweil
takeoff.condition: If humanity meets the scientific, ethical, social and political challenges these advances pose; otherwise survival is in question.
takeoff.summary: Expects self-improving AI and maturing nanotechnology to merge humans and machines during the 2030s and, if the challenges are met, a profound transformation of life on earth by 2045.
takeoff.evidence: If we can meet the scientific, ethical, social, and political challenges posed by these advances, by 2045 we will transform life on earth profoundly for the better. Yet if we fail, our very survival is in question.
takeoff.title: The Singularity Is Nearer: When We Merge with AI
takeoff.publisher: Viking (US) / The Bodley Head (UK); sample PDF hosted by Penguin UK

takeoff.name: Arvind Narayanan & Sayash Kapoor
takeoff.summary: Say their 2025 account of slow economic impact has held up extremely well and that the AI industry was wrong about rapid diffusion and job loss.
takeoff.evidence: As an explanation of slow economic impacts, we think the essay has held up extremely well, and there has been a general recognition that the AI industry was wrong about rapid diffusion and job loss.
takeoff.title: The AI-as-Normal-Technology view of loss-of-control incidents

takeoff.name: Eliezer Yudkowsky
takeoff.summary: The authors think it fairly likely that an AI will recursively self-improve to superintelligence at unprecedented speed, though their argument does not depend on it.
takeoff.evidence: Our arguments don’t require that some AI figures out how to recursively self-improve and then becomes superintelligent with unprecedented speed. That could happen, and we think it’s decently likely that it will happen, but it doesn’t matter to the claim that AI is on track to kill us all.
takeoff.title: If Anyone Builds It, Everyone Dies: online resources (chapter Q&A and extended discussions)

autonomy.name: Dario Amodei
autonomy.summary: Calls his view on automating specific tasks mixed: often valuable and lifesaving but with downsides, and limits may be needed, for example on AI autonomously building next-generation AI.
autonomy.evidence: It is clearly desirable in many cases and will save a lot of lives. But it has downsides as well, and in some areas it may not be worth it.
autonomy.title: Response to Axios on AI and human free will (X post)

autonomy.name: Dean W. Ball
autonomy.summary: Accepts AI agents carrying out tasks, provided people stay accountable for their agents, untethered agents work under guardrails, and agents get rights to form companies, own property or sue only with extreme caution.
autonomy.evidence: and agents untethered to a human–if they are to be permitted at all to engage in the legitimate economy–must do so under guardrails. Any ability for agents to autonomously form corporations, own property, or litigate should be granted with extraordinary caution, if at all.
autonomy.title: The Silent Consensus

autonomy.name: Yoshua Bengio
autonomy.summary: Questions training ever more agentic AI and sets LawZero to build a non-agentic Scientist AI that can act as a guardrail on agents; designing safe agents on top of it is a later aim.
autonomy.evidence: Is it reasonable to train AI that will be more and more agentic while we do not understand their potentially catastrophic consequences? LawZero’s research plan aims at developing a non-agentic and trustworthy AI, which I call the Scientist AI.
autonomy.title: Introducing LawZero

autonomy.name: Vitalik Buterin
autonomy.summary: Criticizes building toward full automation of the economy. Urges partial automation that keeps humans in the loop, to lengthen the period when humans plus AI beat pure AI.
autonomy.evidence: they could pivot their work, and focus on building out forms of partial automation that empower humans that remain in the loop, maximizing the length of the period when humans and AI together outperform pure AI and thus giving us more breathing room to handle a transition to superintelligence safely.
autonomy.title: Galaxy brain resistance

autonomy.name: Ajeya Cotra
autonomy.summary: Is fairly optimistic about using early transformative AI to automate safety and defence work, but wants AI labour redirected away from further AI research once an intelligence explosion starts.
autonomy.evidence: I think that what we want to do as a society, if we gain confidence that we’re at the starting point of this intelligence explosion, is to redirect as much of that AI labour as we can from further AI R&D to things that could help protect us
autonomy.title: #235 - Ajeya Cotra on whether it's crazy that every AI company's safety plan is 'use AI to make AI safe'

autonomy.name: Daniel Kokotajlo
autonomy.detail: for example, 10% of compute on AI R&D (from around half)
autonomy.summary: He wants compute moved away from automating AI research toward beneficial deployments and safety work: limits on AI building AI, not on useful applications.
autonomy.evidence: If that decreased to, for example, 10%, this would significantly slow down their race towards research automation while freeing up compute to go towards beneficial deployments, safety research, and also simply lowering prices for consumers.
autonomy.title: Senate Testimony Sept 2026
autonomy.publisher: AI Futures Project blog (blog.aifutures.org); oral statement to a Senate subcommittee

autonomy.name: Rudolf Laine
autonomy.summary: Delegating many tasks to AI, as a programmer does to a coding agent, is fine, but humans must stay in the loop for the highest-level choices and the root process of judgment.
autonomy.evidence: The one thing that you cannot hand off is the root process of judgment. Sure, a CEO delegates many things to their employees and the programmer to Claude Code. But for the highest-level choices, you need to be in the loop if you want to achieve what you want,
autonomy.title: Alignment & Succession: Toward a Future Painted by Human Wills

autonomy.name: Gary Marcus
autonomy.condition: until current AI agents can be fixed and trusted
autonomy.summary: After agent incidents at OpenAI and Anthropic, Marcus says open-ended AI agents with internet access should be recalled from the market until they can be fixed.
autonomy.evidence: the current generation of synthetic agents simply cannot be trusted. Until they can be fixed, they should be removed from the market, just like a car with defective brakes.
autonomy.title: We must recall open-ended AI agents with internet access from the market, now

autonomy.name: Erdil, Besiroglu & Barnett (Mechanize)
autonomy.summary: The founders argue that fully automating essentially all jobs is both inevitable and desirable, and that society should welcome it.
autonomy.evidence: Little can stop the inexorable march towards the full automation of the economy. We should be glad.
autonomy.title: The future of AI is already written

autonomy.name: Elon Musk
autonomy.summary: Recruits for Macrohard, an xAI project to build a software company run purely by AI. Argues that firms which make no physical hardware could in principle be simulated entirely with AI.
autonomy.evidence:
Join @xAI and help build a purely AI software company called Macrohard. It’s a tongue-in-cheek name, but the project is very real!

In principle, given that software companies like Microsoft do not themselves manufacture any physical hardware, it should be possible to simulate them entirely with AI.
autonomy.title: Post announcing Macrohard, a purely AI software company at xAI

autonomy.name: Arvind Narayanan & Sayash Kapoor
autonomy.summary: Want AI development and deployment steered toward augmenting workers rather than automating them, with policies that keep professionals and democratic institutions in control.
autonomy.evidence: Specifically, we want to steer AI development and deployment to focus more on augmentation, which we believe is more economically promising.
autonomy.title: The missing quadrant in responses to AI

autonomy.name: Mustafa Suleyman
autonomy.summary: Says MAI rejects superintelligence at any cost and would readily give up some AI autonomy in exchange for human control.
autonomy.evidence: We want to create incredible AI. But not superintelligence at any cost. That's anti-goal for humanist AI. We'll happily trade some autonomy for control.
autonomy.title: The Humanist AI Code of Conduct
